messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The night it happened, Marcus was leaving a late dinner with friends in the city. He was fifty-three then, still running his own dental practice, still feeling like he had a handle on things. A patrol car pulled up alongside him as he walked to his car. Two officers jumped out, shouting. Before he could raise his hands or explain he was a dentist, a taxpaying man who had just finished his meal, he was on the ground, his face pressed into the asphalt. He heard the crack of a radio, the grunt of effort, and then the searing pain in his ribs as a knee drove into his side. It was a case of mistaken identity, they said later. A meaningless apology. But Marcus had come to believe that something about him, something intrinsic, had made it happen. *Intrinsic Fault* was a quiet, corrosive certainty that settled into his bones: if he had been a different kind of man, a white man, a man who didn't look like a threat just by existing, the officers would have seen a citizen, not a suspect. What happened was deeply unfair, and nothing had been done about it. *Injustice* wasn't just a thought; it was a pressure in his chest, a grinding resentment that made his jaw ache even before he climbed into his dental chair each morning. He felt that his life had been destroyed by the trauma — *Life Destroyed* — and he often caught himself staring at his own reflection in the operatory mirror, wondering if the man who used to joke with his hygienist was ever coming back.

The memory of that night felt alien, like a film he had been forced to watch rather than something he had lived. *Memory Feels Alien* — he sometimes told his partner that it was like remembering a story about someone else, except this story came with sounds: the *Auditory Recall* of the officer's boots scraping the pavement, the sharp bark of commands. And it came with pain. When the memory returned, often without warning, he felt a phantom ache in his ribs, the same spot where the knee had pinned him down. *Pain Recall* was visceral and humiliating, and it made him feel like he was still on that asphalt. This feeling of the memory being unreal and yet physically present made the negative appraisals worse — *Memory → Negative Appraisals* — because if the memory wasn't even his, how could he ever make sense of it? How could he prove it happened? The injustice felt more profound, his sense of being destroyed more absolute, when the event itself felt like a ghost story he couldn't escape.

Because of these intrusive, painful memories, Marcus began to change how he lived. *Memory → Maladaptive Strategies* — the sounds and the rib pain drove him to avoid anything that could trigger them. He stopped walking anywhere at night. He avoided all feelings, positive or negative. *Avoid All Feelings* was his way of staying safe: if he didn't feel the anger, he couldn't feel the shame. If he didn't feel the love from his partner, he couldn't feel the terror of losing it all. He also avoided anything stressful — *Avoid Stressors* — which meant canceling appointments with anxious patients, delegating difficult procedures to his associate, and gradually shrinking his practice to only the most predictable, low-stakes cases. He started *Checking Surroundings* constantly: every time he entered a room, he mapped the exits, noted the windows, catalogued the faces.

The threat he felt from strangers was pervasive and exhausting. *Threat from Strangers* meant that even a patient walking toward the reception desk made his shoulders tighten. A delivery driver at the back door sent his heart racing. He felt threatened by strangers approaching him even in ordinary situations — a person asking for directions, a neighbor saying hello — and he had developed a habit of *Safe Seat Seeking*: he always chose where to sit based on how safe or protected he felt. In restaurants, his back to a wall. In waiting rooms, a seat with a clear view of the door. At home, he sat on the side of the couch farthest from the windows. This constant vigilance, this scanning for threat, made the memory more accessible — *Threat → Memory* — because every time his heart pounded at an approaching stranger, his brain seemed to say, *Yes, this is what it felt like.* And the memory, in turn, reinforced the threat — *Memory → Threat* — because the pain in his ribs and the sound of boots were proof that danger was real, that it had happened once and could happen again.

The threat also strengthened his negative appraisals. *Threat → Negative Appraisals* — the more he felt threatened by strangers, the more he was certain that something about him had caused the event, that the world saw him as a target. The injustice burned hotter when he was scanning a crowd, because he could see the casual way other people walked, unaware, unafraid. He knew, logically, that not every stranger was a threat, but his body didn't believe it. His body believed that the world was divided into safe and unsafe, and that he was marked.

His maladaptive strategies, in turn, fed back into the memory and the appraisals. *Maladaptive Strategies → Memory* — avoiding all feelings and checking his surroundings meant he was always on alert, and that state of hypervigilance made the memory more likely to surface, as if his brain was saying, *You're scanning for danger, so here's the danger you're looking for.* And *Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals* — the more he avoided, the more he confirmed to himself that his life really was destroyed, that he was too broken to function normally, that the injustice had permanently reshaped him. He had stopped going to his niece's birthday parties. He had stopped having dinner with friends. He told himself it was to avoid stress, but underneath, he was certain that the man who used to laugh at those parties was gone, and that nothing would bring him back.

What finally brought Marcus to seek help was a moment in his own office. A patient, a middle-aged man, walked in wearing a dark uniform. Marcus froze in the hallway, his hand on the door to the operatory. The man was a postal worker, just dropping off a package, but for a few seconds Marcus saw the patrol car, heard the boots. He turned and walked back to his office, closed the door, and sat in the dark for ten minutes. That night, he told his partner he couldn't keep living like this. He was afraid of what he was becoming — a man who was afraid of his own shadow, a dentist who couldn't face a patient in a blue shirt. He was hoping, though he wouldn't say it out loud, that someone could help him find a way to feel like himself again, or at least to stop the pain in his ribs from coming back every time he heard a loud noise.
